analysis.one_liner: Puts everyone into a government health plan with no deductibles, funded by taxes on high earners and corporations.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of the 118th Congress with one cosponsor, the bill was sent to six committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would move nearly all Americans into a new public health insurance program, Medicare for America, after a two-year transition. Coverage would be automatic for almost everyone, include dental, vision, hearing, and long-term home care, charge no deductibles, cap yearly out-of-pocket costs at $3,500 per person, and base premiums on income. It would pay for this by letting the 2017 Republican tax cuts expire, adding taxes on high earners, corporations, alcohol, tobacco, and sugary drinks, and forcing drug makers to accept government-negotiated prices. Private insurers could not sell coverage that duplicates the public plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly everyone: all U.S. residents would be automatically enrolled, with the biggest gains for the uninsured, low- and middle-income households, people with disabilities (who lose the 24-month Medicare waiting period), and anyone who needs dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care that most plans don't cover. Small employers get a low-cost option to enroll workers.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a temporary public health plan on the ACA exchanges for 2025 and 2026, with $0 premiums for people under 200% of the poverty line and premiums capped at 8% of income for everyone else.

Starting in 2026-2027, automatically enrolls nearly every U.S. resident in Medicare for America, covering the full Medicare and Medicaid benefit lists plus dental, hearing, vision, home- and community-based long-term care, family planning including abortion, and gender-confirming care.

Eliminates deductibles entirely, caps annual out-of-pocket costs at $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household (or $0 for low-income households), bans balance billing and surprise charges, and forbids prior-authorization and step-therapy hurdles.
Ends the 24-month waiting period before disabled people can get Medicare, and removes Medicare Advantage bonus payments and plans' ability to drop providers mid-year.

Requires the government to negotiate drug prices and, if a maker refuses an acceptable price, authorizes competitors to license the drug's patents for public supply — plus a moratorium on direct-to-consumer drug advertising.
Pays hospitals at least 110% of Medicare rates and providers the higher of Medicare or Medicaid rates, with the federal government covering the Medicaid rate gap for states through 2031.

Funds the program by letting the 2017 tax law (Public Law 115-97) sunset, adding a surtax and increased Medicare payroll and investment-income taxes on high earners, and new excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugared drinks.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and corporations, who lose the 2017 tax cuts and face new surtaxes and Medicare taxes; consumers of tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks, who pay new excise taxes; brand-name drug makers, whose prices would be set by negotiation or licensing; and private insurers and brokers, whose market for duplicative coverage would be largely eliminated. Employers with 100+ employees would have to offer qualifying coverage or make firm-wide contributions to the public plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: Coverage is not free: premiums would still rise to 8% of income, and out-of-pocket costs would reach $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household above 200% of the poverty line.
New excise taxes on alcohol, tobacco, and sugared drinks raise prices that consumers pay at the register, falling hardest on lower-income buyers of those products.

The transition is enormous: Medicaid and CHIP wind down through 2033, ACA exchanges end in 2031, and insurers are barred from selling duplicative coverage — a wholesale restructuring of how Americans get insurance, with real disruption risk.

The bill is weaker than full single-payer: it lets private insurers continue selling Medicare Advantage for America plans inside the program, paid 95% of public rates, preserving a private-profiting layer.

Providers and employers bear adjustment costs: providers would be paid Medicare-linked rates rather than private-insurance rates, and Members of Congress and their staff would be enrolled in the public plan alongside everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is the largest expansion of health coverage since Medicare itself: universal eligibility, no deductibles, hard out-of-pocket caps, and dental, vision, hearing, and long-term care most plans don't include. The costs are real — broad new taxes on high earners and everyday purchases, the elimination of the conventional private insurance market, and a multi-year transition with genuine disruption risk. The bill also hedges by keeping Medicare Advantage insurers inside the program at reduced rates, which blunts savings but softens industry opposition. On balance it is a major transfer of resources toward ordinary households, paid for substantially by the wealthy and by health industries — but it never came close to being tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last days of a lame-duck session, referred to six committees, and none of them ever took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Medicare for America Act of 2024 on December 19, 2024, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky as its only cosponsor — thirteen days before the 118th Congress ended.

The same day, it was referred to six committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, the Judiciary, Natural Resources, Education and the Workforce, and House Administration — the standard first step that gives committees control over whether a bill advances.
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action after the referral; the bill expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers and brand-name drug makers kept the health market exactly as it is; high earners and corporations avoided the new taxes; and the House's six committee chairs never had to take a public position. People without affordable coverage gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested; both sponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill went to committees run by the Republican House majority with two weeks left in the session.

industries.note: The bill would largely eliminate their core business by banning sale of coverage that duplicates the public plan and sunsetting the ACA exchanges and most employer-based coverage. But it entrenches them inside the new program as Medicare Advantage for America plans paid 95% of public rates, keeping insurers as the managed-care channel for anyone who opts for them.

Drug prices would be set by government negotiation, and if a maker refuses, the government can license its patents to competing manufacturers, with an interim cap tied to prices in other wealthy countries. A moratorium on direct-to-consumer drug advertising and a prescription-drug review board add further pressure on their pricing power.

Hospitals would be guaranteed at least 110% of Medicare rates and providers the higher of Medicare or Medicaid rates, with the federal government covering the Medicaid rate gap through 2031 — a raise over Medicaid — but they would lose the higher payments private insurance pays today and face site-neutral payments and a ban on balance billing.

Bonus payments to Medicare Advantage plans are repealed, plans could no longer drop providers mid-year to cut costs, and any future private plans would be paid only 95% of public rates and barred from paying broker fees.
Supplemental plans and Medicare Advantage for America plans would be prohibited from paying broker fees, removing a commission stream built into today's system.
The bill sunsets the 2017 tax-cut law, adds a surtax, raises the Medicare payroll and net investment income taxes, and ends health-savings-account deductions to fund universal coverage.
